relations.myth: Quest for the Water of Life
relations.note: Khidr serves as minister, guide, or vanguard commander during the immortality quest.

relations.myth: Khidr discovers and drinks the Water of Life
relations.note: Khidr gains immortality from the spring that Dhul-Qarnayn unsuccessfully seeks.
Some healing tales make Khidr assist, parallel, or supersede Lokman.
Alexander and ʿAntarah appear as parallel heralds of monotheistic change.

god_relations.note: Late visionary and storytelling traditions sometimes pair Khidr with Gabriel.

god_relations.myth: Angel reveals the Water of Life
god_relations.note: The angelic companion tells Dhul-Qarnayn about the Water of Life.
In some unstable recensions, the angel gives Dhul-Qarnayn a wondrous stone.
Some later Islamic retellings identify their added angelic guardian as Gabriel.

Abraham.note: One strand makes Khidr Abraham's contemporary and follower.

Abraham.myth: Embracing Abraham’s faith and circumambulating the Kaʿba
Abraham.note: Dhul-Qarnayn allegedly accepts Abraham’s faith and circumambulates the Kaʿba with him.

Aesop.note: Aesop’s slave biography, traits, anecdotes, and fables were transferred to Luqmān.

Alexander.myth: Quest for the Water of Life
Alexander.note: Khidr serves as guide, minister, scout, or cook while Alexander seeks immortality.

Alexander the Great.note: Early and medieval interpreters identify Dhul-Qarnayn with the legendary Macedonian conqueror.

Allah/God.note: God grants Luqmān wisdom and commands him to be grateful.

Allāh.note: ʿAntarah invokes Allāh in transmitted poetry and the Islamicized epic.

Andreas.myth: Cook discovers the Water of Life
Andreas.note: Islamic Alexander traditions equate Khidr narratively with Alexander's immortalized cook.

Angels.note: Angels offer Luqmān rule or judgment and communicate his gift of wisdom.

Arpachshad.note: One medieval genealogy places Arpachshad in Khidr's ancestral line.

Balaam son of Beor.note: Luqmān’s constructed patronymic Bāʿūrāʾ prompted identification or confusion with Balaam.

Cyrus the Great.note: Modern Muslim interpreters identify him with Cyrus through empire and two-horned symbolism.

Dhū al-Qarnayn “the Elder”.myth: Quest for the River of Life
Dhū al-Qarnayn “the Elder”.note: Khidr serves in his vanguard and discovers the River of Life.

Dāwūd/David.note: Luqmān silently watches David fashion armor and learns its purpose.
Some traditions make Luqmān David’s counselor, vizier, or earlier judge.
David receives kingship while Luqmān receives wisdom without its judicial ordeal.

God.myth: Divine gift of mercy and hidden knowledge
God.note: God grants Khidr mercy and special knowledge and directs his actions.
Majnun asks God to increase or perpetuate his love instead of curing it.
God hears their prayer, guides and preserves them, then awakens them as a sign.

God/Allah.myth: Commission, journeys, judgment, and construction of the barrier
God/Allah.note: God grants him power and means, authorizes judgment, and promises the barrier’s destruction.

Gul-Nazar.note: Gul-Nazar grants Antar the joys of vengeance, power, and love.

Hidden Imam.note: Some Shiʿi traditions make Khidr the Hidden Imam's companion and precedent for prolonged occult life.

Ibrāhīm.note: Learned epic theology places ʿAntarah within sacred history beginning with Ibrāhīm.

Ibrāhīm/Abraham.note: A learned genealogy inserts Luqmān into Abraham’s extended family through Nahor and Terah.

Ishmael.note: Ishmael appears beside Abraham and Dhul-Qarnayn in later Kaʿba traditions.

Jesus.note: Theological and Sufi systems group Khidr with Jesus among living or eschatological prophets.

Jesus Christ.note: The sleepers confess Christ and accept persecution rather than sacrifice to pagan gods.
Jesus Christ.source: Jacob of Serugh; Gregory of Tours

Jhūlelāl.note: Sindhi traditions overlap Khidr with Jhūlelāl and related river-protector identities.

Layla.myth: Reciprocal love, separation, messages, and swoons
Layla.note: Majnun and Layla love one another but are separated by her family.

Layla.myth: Death at Layli’s grave and paradisal reunion
Layla.note: Majnun dies embracing Layli’s grave; they are buried together and reunited in Paradise.

Lubad.note: Lubad’s final collapse signals the end of Luqmān’s allotted lifespan.

Malkān.note: One medieval genealogy names Khidr, as Baliyā, the son of Malkān.

Maʾjūj.myth: Construction of the barrier against Gog and Magog
Maʾjūj.note: Dhul-Qarnayn constructs an iron-and-copper barrier to contain the corrupting people.

Moses.note: Khidr teaches Moses through three troubling acts before explaining them and separating.

Moses.myth: Coordination with the Moses and divine servant episode
Moses.note: Later texts conflate or coordinate Moses’s preceding Qur’anic episode with Dhul-Qarnayn’s cycle.

Muḥammad.note: Weak later reports claim that Khidr attended Muhammad's funeral.
The epic makes ʿAntarah foretell Muḥammad’s coming without meeting him.

Noah.note: One genealogy traces Khidr from Malkān through Arpachshad and Shem to Noah.

Pharaoh’s daughter.note: A competing medieval report makes Khidr the son of Pharaoh's daughter.

Qitmir.note: The dog accompanies or guards the sleepers, stretching its forelegs at the cave entrance.

Sheikh Tāhir.note: Sindhi traditions variously identify the Uderolāl saint as Sheikh Tāhir or Khidr.

Shem.note: One medieval genealogy makes Khidr a descendant of Shem.

Yaʾjūj.myth: Construction of the barrier against Gog and Magog
Yaʾjūj.note: Dhul-Qarnayn constructs an iron-and-copper barrier to contain the corrupting people.

seven vultures.note: Luqmān raises seven successive birds whose lifespans measure his prodigious longevity.

Āzar/Terah.note: Later genealogy makes Terah an ancestor of Luqmān through Nahor and Bāʿūrāʾ.

Şahmaran.note: Lokman gains medical knowledge through Şahmaran’s death or medicinal flesh.

Ṣaʿb ibn Dhī Marāthid.note: Yemeni tradition identifies Dhul-Qarnayn as a Himyarite Tubbaʿ named Ṣaʿb.
